name: Dental sandpaper strips

lead: Dental sandpaper strips are gritty strips sold online to scrape surface stain from teeth, for a lighter look. They are distinct from peroxide whitening strips, which use a chemical bleaching agent.

They remove stain by mechanical abrasion and cannot change the intrinsic colour of the tooth. Dentists remove extrinsic stain by scaling and polishing with abrasive pastes, an in-office procedure that removes roughly one micron of enamel per treatment. No studies of consumer abrasive strips were found.

paras: Users rub a strip across the front surfaces of the teeth for a short time, as an occasional stain-removal step. Others get a professional scale and polish instead, which uses abrasive pastes under a dentist's control.
Dental literature lists abrasion as a cause of tooth wear, and enamel does not regrow. The abrasivity of these strips is not standardised.

angle.text: Online marketplaces sell abrasive strips for scraping surface stain off teeth, distinct from peroxide strips. They work by rubbing stain away, the same principle as a professional polish but without controlled abrasivity. No studies or standard abrasivity data exist for them.

lead: Dental sandpaper strips, also sold as teeth sanding strips, are thin abrasive strips found on online marketplaces that are promoted for rubbing surface stains off teeth. The pitch is a whiter-looking smile through mechanical scraping, in the same spirit as an abrasive whitening toothpaste or a professional polish, but with a gritty strip applied by hand.[1][2]

The route to a brighter smile is removal of extrinsic stain, the coloured film that sits on the tooth surface. Coffee, tea, red wine, cola and tobacco tar are the usual causes, and most extrinsic stains come off with cleaning, either at home with an abrasive whitening toothpaste or professionally through scaling and polishing.[3] Stains that sit inside the tooth are intrinsic, and abrasion of the surface does not change them.[2][3]

No published study of consumer sandpaper strips exists, and the abrasivity of these products is not standardised; dental references discuss abrasion mainly in connection with toothpaste and professional polishing.[1][4][5]

paras: The strips carry an abrasive grit similar in concept to fine sandpaper and are promoted for rubbing off coffee, tea or tobacco stain.[3] Their grit and abrasivity are not standardised.

sections.h: Tooth stain and how it is normally removed
paras: Extrinsic discoloration is staining on the outer tooth surface. Tea, especially black tea with its theaflavins and tannins, coffee, red wine and cola can stain with regular use; tobacco tar builds a yellow-brown-black film near the gumline; and plaque can take on colour when certain bacteria produce pigment. Some mouthwashes, such as chlorhexidine, can bind to tannins from tea or coffee.[3] Wikipedia notes that a stain left in place for a long time can eventually become intrinsic, and that preventing recurrence means addressing the cause, such as quitting smoking.[3]

Whitening toothpastes remove surface stains mainly through abrasion, and some also contain peroxide or agents such as sodium tripolyphosphate that help break down stain. Using them twice daily typically shows results in two to four weeks, and a 2017 systematic review found that nearly all whitening dentifrices reduced extrinsic stain whether or not they contained a bleaching agent.[1] They cannot change a tooth's natural colour or reverse discoloration from deeper stains or decay.[1][2]

Abrasives make up roughly 8 to 20 percent of a typical toothpaste and include silicas, calcium carbonate, aluminium hydroxide, sodium bicarbonate and hydroxyapatite. Their abrasiveness is rated on the Relative Dentin Abrasivity (RDA) scale; toothpastes above 250 could damage tooth surfaces, and the ANSI and the ADA treat those below 250 as safe and effective for lifelong use.[1] No such rating exists for consumer sanding strips.

Professional prophylaxis polishes with abrasive paste and is reported to remove about one micron of enamel per treatment. Selective polishing is now recommended by many educational institutions over routine full-mouth polishing, because polishing is largely cosmetic.[6]

Abrasion is defined in the tooth wear literature as tooth loss from physical means other than tooth contact, with high-abrasivity toothpaste listed among its contributing factors.[5] Whitening toothpastes contain more abrasives and detergents than regular ones, and excessive use may damage enamel.[1][2] Enamel is not regenerated by the body.[4]
